items.headline: Opinion: Limb girdle muscular dystrophy patients face a maddening reality
items.preview: Patients with limb girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD) are facing delays in treatment due to regulatory issues.
items.article:
The author discusses the challenges faced by LGMD patients in accessing timely treatments, particularly in light of recent FDA actions that have created uncertainty in drug development. 
Why this matters: The delays in treatment not only hinder progress in clinical trials but also lead to irreversible muscle loss for patients waiting for therapies. 
The piece highlights the need for regulatory reforms to ensure that innovative therapies can reach patients without unnecessary delays, emphasizing the urgency for those living with progressive rare diseases.

items.headline: J&J nabs option to buy ‘in vivo’ CAR-T maker Sail for nearly $2.6B
items.preview: Johnson & Johnson is set to invest in Sail Biomedicines, focusing on in vivo cell therapy.
items.article:
Johnson & Johnson has announced a significant investment in Sail Biomedicines, which specializes in in vivo cell therapy, with an initial payment of $785 million. 
This investment aims to advance Sail's lead program, SAIL-0839, which is still in preclinical testing. 
J&J has secured an option to acquire Sail for $2.58 billion in the future, indicating a strong interest in expanding its presence in the cell therapy market.

items.headline: Advances in AI-designed base editors pave the way for next-generation gene therapy
items.preview: A research team has developed AI-designed base editors that significantly improve gene-editing efficiency.
items.article:
Researchers have created 'OpenABE', a new class of adenine base editors that enhance gene-editing efficiency by up to 36-fold compared to traditional methods. 
This advancement is crucial for treating genetic diseases, as it allows for precise editing of both nuclear and mitochondrial DNA. 
Why this matters: The improved safety and efficiency of these editors could accelerate the development of effective therapies for previously intractable genetic disorders.

items.headline: Meeting unmet needs: new treatments for gout race in the clinic
items.preview: New therapies for gout are being developed to address the needs of patients who do not respond to existing treatments.
items.article:
With nearly half of gout patients not adequately treated by current therapies, biotechs are exploring new options, including a second-line therapy called dotinurad. 
This drug aims to provide an effective oral option for patients who cannot tolerate existing treatments. 
Why this matters: The development of new gout treatments is critical for improving patient outcomes and addressing the significant unmet needs in this population.

items.headline: Editorial Note: A nonenzymatic dependency on inositol-requiring enzyme 1 controls cancer cell cycle progression and tumor growth
items.preview: An editorial note addresses errors in a previously published study regarding cancer cell cycle progression.
items.article:
This editorial note corrects errors in a previously published article about the role of inositol-requiring enzyme 1 in cancer cell cycle progression. 
The note clarifies issues related to figures and funding statements. 
Why this matters: Accurate reporting in scientific literature is essential for maintaining trust and integrity in research.
